title: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every subarray's absolute sum directly versus running Kadane's Algorithm twice, once mirrored for a minimum.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, find the maximum possible ABSOLUTE VALUE of the sum of any contiguous subarray (the subarray may be empty, contributing a sum of 0).

blocks.caption: Run Kadane's twice, once for the most positive sum and once for the most negative, then combine

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, find the largest possible absolute value of the sum of any contiguous subarray (the empty subarray, contributing 0, is also allowed).

blocks.title: Analogy: The Biggest Swing, Up or Down
blocks.text: Like tracking net elevation change along a trail and asking: what's the single biggest SWING achievable over any continuous stretch, whether that swing is the tallest climb or the deepest drop? Both directions matter equally, so the trail needs to be checked for its best climb and its worst drop separately, then whichever swing is bigger (in magnitude) wins.

blocks.caption: The answer is whichever of the two Kadane's runs (max-sum or min-sum) has the larger magnitude

blocks.text: Edge case: nums has only one element

When nums has exactly one element, the only non-empty subarrays are that single element, so the answer is simply the absolute value of that element (or 0, if considering the empty subarray and the element is somehow not beneficial, though a single element's absolute value is always >= 0).
Before checking every subarray's sum and its absolute value directly, notice the answer must come from one of exactly two extremes: the most positive possible sum, or the most negative possible sum.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The absolute value of any subarray sum is maximized either by making the sum as POSITIVE as possible, or as NEGATIVE as possible, whichever magnitude turns out larger.

Observation 2: Finding the most positive possible subarray sum is exactly the standard Maximum Subarray problem, solvable with Kadane's Algorithm.

Observation 3: Finding the most negative possible subarray sum is the exact mirror: run a Kadane's-style recurrence that tracks a running MINIMUM (extend or restart, keeping whichever is smaller) instead of a maximum.

Observation 4: Track both running values (best-ending-here for max, and best-ending-here for min) simultaneously in a single pass, and combine the overall best positive sum and the absolute value of the overall best negative sum at the end.

Recognizing that a "maximum absolute value" problem often decomposes into "maximum" and "minimum" sub-problems, both solvable by the same underlying technique, is a broadly reusable insight.
This is Kadane's Algorithm run twice in parallel: once in its standard form (tracking a maximum), and once mirrored (tracking a minimum), combined at the end by comparing magnitudes.
For every possible starting index, extend forward one element at a time, tracking the running sum and its absolute value directly.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, accumulating a running sum.
Compare the absolute value of every intermediate running sum against the best found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh running sum is used for every starting position, since each independent walk accumulates its own subarray sum.
abs(total) is compared against best at every intermediate step, since the maximum-magnitude subarray for a given start could occur partway through, either on the positive or negative side.
best is initialized to 0, correctly allowing the empty subarray as a valid (zero-magnitude) baseline.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray sum's absolute value is checked directly, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the n starting positions walks forward up to n elements.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: restarting the running sum from scratch at every new starting position ignores that both the best positive and best negative subarray sums ending at any position only depend on the position just before it, exactly like standard Kadane's Algorithm.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts its running sum from scratch at every starting position. Instead, run two Kadane's-style recurrences simultaneously: maxEnding tracks the best (most positive) subarray sum ending at the current position, and minEnding tracks the best (most negative) subarray sum ending there, using the mirrored recurrence min(x, minEnding + x). At every step, compare the overall best answer against both maxEnding and the negation of minEnding.

Maintain maxEnding and minEnding, both initialized to 0 (allowing the empty subarray). At each element x, update maxEnding = max(x, maxEnding + x) and minEnding = min(x, minEnding + x). Update best to the maximum of its current value, maxEnding, and -minEnding.
Run two Kadane's-style running values in parallel: one tracking the most positive sum ending here, one tracking the most negative.

codes.python:
def max_absolute_sum(nums):
    max_ending = 0                                                          # best (most positive) subarray sum ending here
    min_ending = 0                                                          # best (most negative) subarray sum ending here
    best = 0
    for x in nums:
        max_ending = max(x, max_ending + x)                                 # standard Kadane's, tracking the most positive running sum
        min_ending = min(x, min_ending + x)                                 # mirrored Kadane's, tracking the most negative running sum
        best = max(best, max_ending, -min_ending)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_absolute_sum([1, -3, 2, 3, -4]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass tracking both running values, with O(1) work per element.
Space: O(1) extra.

The absolute value of a subarray's sum is maximized by whichever extreme, most positive or most negative, has the larger magnitude. Since both extremes independently satisfy the same "best value ending here depends only on the immediately preceding position" property that makes standard Kadane's Algorithm work, tracking both simultaneously and combining them at the end covers every possibility in one linear pass.

The two recurrences are mirror images of each other: max(x, maxEnding + x) versus min(x, minEnding + x).
best is updated by comparing against both maxEnding directly and the negation of minEnding, since minEnding itself is a negative number whose magnitude is what actually matters.

blocks.text: Recognizing that "maximum absolute value" decomposes into "maximum" and "minimum" sub-problems, both solvable by the same Kadane's recurrence mirrored in direction, is a broadly reusable insight whenever a problem asks for an extreme magnitude rather than a signed extreme.

items: Running only the standard (maximum) Kadane's pass and forgetting that the most negative subarray sum could have a larger magnitude.
Comparing maxEnding and minEnding directly instead of negating minEnding before comparing, which would incorrectly always favor the positive side.
Initializing maxEnding/minEnding to nums[0] instead of 0, which would incorrectly disallow the empty subarray as a valid (zero) baseline, since this problem explicitly allows it.

items: Explicitly connect this problem to standard Maximum Subarray before coding, framing it as "run Kadane's twice, once mirrored", since recognizing the decomposition is the entire crux of this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximum ABSOLUTE VALUE of a subarray sum" points toward running Kadane's Algorithm twice: once for the maximum sum, once (mirrored) for the minimum sum, then comparing magnitudes.

items: How would you also report which subarray (max-side or min-side) achieved the answer, and its indices? Track tentative start indices for both running values, resetting them on a restart, and record whichever side's magnitude wins at the end.

Does this technique generalize to other "extreme magnitude" problems? Yes, whenever a problem asks for an extreme absolute value derived from a quantity that itself has a standard maximizing (or minimizing) algorithm, running both directions and combining is a reusable strategy.

What if the empty subarray were NOT allowed? The initial values of maxEnding and minEnding would need to start at nums[0] instead of 0, exactly as in the standard (non-absolute) Maximum Subarray problem.

A direct extension of Maximum Subarray, running the same Kadane's recurrence twice (once mirrored for a minimum), a pattern also seen conceptually in problems requiring both a "best case" and "worst case" swept in a single pass.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (dual Kadane's): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Dual Kadane's Algorithm: a running maximum-ending-here and a running minimum-ending-here, tracked simultaneously
Core Idea: The maximum absolute subarray sum is whichever has the larger magnitude: the best positive sum, or the best negative sum
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: "Maximum absolute value" decomposes into a maximum sub-problem and a mirrored minimum sub-problem, both solvable by the same underlying recurrence
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Run Kadane's twice (max and min), answer is the larger magnitude of the two
